source.title: Deep Network Trainability via Persistent Subspace Orthogonality
source.authors: Alex Massucco; D. Murari; C. Schönlieb

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present, including appendices and experimental setup.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares initializations and depth, reporting classification accuracy as evidence about trainability. It does not measure training classification error, so its results test trainability conceptually rather than the versions’ exact training-error outcomes.
record.gate_note: The paper reports test/validation accuracy, not training classification error. Those accuracy results do not establish whether training error reached zero or near zero. Reported numbers used below are the study’s accuracy outcomes; cited results from other work are not included.
record.test_reason: The study tests V4's initialization–trainable-depth relationship through controlled initialization and depth comparisons in plain networks, supported by analysis of gradient preservation. Its accuracy measurements provide indirect evidence of trainability, not training-error or convergence-speed measurements. It does not test V3's batch-normalized convolutional-network training-error comparison.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate. The authors propose persistent subspace orthogonality as a mechanism for preserving gradient components across depth and report improved trainability from initializations satisfying it. They find that maintaining PSO during training is unnecessary in their experiments. Their stronger language describing PSO as necessary should be attributed to them; the experiments do not establish universal necessity.
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes persistent subspace orthogonality and compares custom shared or structured orthogonal initializations with Kaiming and independent orthogonal initialization. It does not reproduce the original methods in the claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Depth and initialization scheme affect reported test accuracy. The CIFAR-10 experiment also varies learning rate, but its figure reports test accuracy rather than training error.

fits_no_version.finding: Structured residual initializations outperform Kaiming and independent orthogonal initializations in fully connected MNIST models; their accuracy nevertheless declines at greater depth.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Initialization structure affects the performance and stability of deep fully connected residual networks.

fits_no_version.finding: Fashion-MNIST limit models with non-affine modifications achieve validation accuracies comparable to the exactly orthogonal residual baseline in Table 4.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: These modified convolutional residual architectures remain practically trainable through 200 layers under the tested recipes.

record.problems: The experiments report test or validation accuracy rather than training classification error. The MNIST depth experiments use five seeds and report maximum absolute deviations; the CIFAR-10 learning-rate comparison is presented as a figure without tabulated values. MNIST is not one of the benchmark datasets named in the versions.
record.rows_left_out: No results omitted from the extracted rows. Other reported accuracy results (including the residual 5-layer condition, alternative activation functions, projection/block subspace sweeps, Fashion-MNIST ablations, and CIFAR-10 learning-rate curves) were not rowed because they do not directly measure the versions’ specified training-error outcomes.

untested.parts: Near-zero training classification error on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100, random labels, model-size effects, and regularized or early-stopped training.
Teacher–student ReLU optimization, spurious local minima, and extra student neurons.
Training-error degradation in plain batch-normalized convolutional networks, matched identity-shortcut controls, longer training, deep plain tanh networks, and Fixup.

Direct learning-speed or convergence-time measurements; training-error trajectories; matched-variance Gaussian versus orthogonal initialization in deep tanh networks; and 10,000-layer convolutional networks.
Initial linearized stability limits, catapult dynamics, curvature and sharpness evolution, and threshold-related divergence.
Batch-normalization speed and learning-rate comparisons, and Fixup training without normalization.

record.verdict_notes: The record incorrectly treats missing training-error measurements as disqualifying all V4 evidence: V4 also concerns initialization-dependent trainable depth. Conversely, accuracy declines alone do not justify its blanket limits_scope verdict. Independent orthogonal matrices do not satisfy the claimed cross-layer gradient-preservation condition, so their failures do not challenge that conditional claim. States for r3–r11 describe the initialization effect in matched comparisons, not successful learning by every comparator. All tabulated accuracy values and reported maximum-deviation uncertainties match the supplied text. The omitted activation, projection, and CIFAR-10 comparisons are already declared in rows_left_out. Excerpt E3 concerns Figure 3's block/projection experiments and should not be attached to r11, r22, or r23.

versions.untested_parts: CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 training error, corrupted or random labels, SGD/Adam training-error outcomes, smaller models and early stopping effects.
Two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems, spurious minima, and student width relative to teacher width.

The paper compares feedforward and residual architectures over depth, but reports test accuracy rather than training error; it does not test batch-normalized convolutional networks, ImageNet, or longer training to assess whether training error remains elevated.

It tests initialization and depth in its own architectures, but does not measure training speed directly or test the cited Glorot, He, Schoenholz, Pennington, or Xiao recipes as stated in the version.
No stability-limit learning-rate sweep, loss-rise/curvature-drop mechanism, sharpness threshold, or divergence analysis.
No batch-normalization comparison or Fixup experiment.

relationships.condition: Plain width-64 MNIST ReLU networks, depths 50–200, trained with Adam for 20 epochs
relationships.reason: Rows r3–r11 show shared orthogonal initialization retaining approximately 97% test accuracy while Kaiming deteriorates to approximately 10–12% and independent orthogonal initialization fails at depths 100–200. The authors explicitly interpret this contrast as improved trainability; the evidence concerns trainable depth indirectly, not measured convergence speed.
relationships.display_finding: Shared orthogonal initialization retained approximately 97% test accuracy, while Kaiming deteriorated to approximately 10–12% and independent orthogonal initialization failed at depths 100–200.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: MNIST feedforward and residual models at depths 50–200 under the tested initialization schemes
reader_labels.reason: Initialization and depth materially changed test accuracy: shared orthogonal feedforward models retained high accuracy at depth 200 (r11), while Kaiming and independent orthogonal comparisons had low accuracy or diverged at greater depths (r6–r10, r16–r23). These results do not directly report training error or training speed.
